strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper provides both empirical (Fig. 2, MoG and Stokes experiments) and theoretical (Appendix B.3, Theorems B.1/B.2) evidence for the 'Jensen's Gap' that arises when PDE constraints are imposed on the posterior mean E[x0|xt] rather than the final sample, giving a solid conceptual foundation for the proposed method.

The proposed fix (post-hoc distillation with physics loss applied directly to the final student output) is simple, well-justified, and effectively sidesteps the identified theoretical issue rather than just heuristically mitigating it.

Extensive empirical validation across a wide range of PDE benchmarks (Darcy, Poisson, Burgers, Helmholtz, Stokes, Heat, Navier–Stokes, Porous Medium, Stefan) and downstream tasks (forward, inverse, reconstruction), with consistent improvements in both accuracy and PDE-residual satisfaction over strong recent baselines (PIDM, DiffusionPDE, ECI-sampling, D-Flow).

Strong efficiency gains are convincingly demonstrated via compute-matched comparisons (Table 3), showing PIDDM achieves better or comparable quality at a small fraction of the NFEs/wall-clock time of baselines.

Thorough ablation studies (component attribution, distillation backbone choice, diversity preservation via SWD/APDD, teacher-quality and architecture robustness, dynamic weighting, latent-optimization stability) substantially strengthen the empirical case and address plausible reviewer concerns.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper explicitly notes that its distributional fidelity claims remain empirical rather than proven, and discusses dependency on teacher quality and PDE residual operator reliability.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Appendix B.3) is restricted to a toy linear/Gaussian setting with a linear score parameterization; while illustrative, its connection to the nonlinear, high-dimensional PDE settings used in experiments is not formally established, so the explanatory power for real experiments remains largely intuitive/empirical.

Despite explicitly discussing Physics-Informed Distillation (PID, Tee et al. 2024) as closely related work with a similar name, the paper does not include it as an empirical baseline, leaving a gap in the comparison against the most conceptually adjacent prior method.

Fairness of baseline tuning is unclear: several baselines (DiffusionPDE, PIDM) are given the same λ as PIDDM's λtrain rather than being independently tuned, which could understate their best achievable performance and slightly favor the proposed method.

The teacher diffusion model itself is trained without any physics constraint, so the student's constraint satisfaction and distributional fidelity depend heavily on the quality/coverage of the teacher's samples; sensitivity analysis of this dependency (Table 8) is only conducted on a single dataset (Darcy).

Most additional diagnostic ablations (diversity, teacher robustness, dynamic weighting, latent optimization stability) are conducted only on the Darcy dataset, limiting generality of these conclusions to the other seven PDE benchmarks used elsewhere in the paper.

The total computational cost of the pipeline (teacher training + trajectory generation for distillation data + student distillation) is not clearly aggregated against baseline training costs, so the 'lower computation' claim, while true at inference time, could be presented more transparently for the full training pipeline.
